lead: Analog pulse modulation sends a narrow pulse again and again. The message rides on one pulse property: height in PAM, width in PWM, or position in PPM. The receiver looks only at that property. The pulse period T<sub>s</sub> stays fixed; only one pulse parameter carries the message. The circuit stays simple. PAM is the first step towards PCM; PWM and PPM are used in cheap control links, lamp dimming, servo signals and optical pulse links. Here you see how each is made, what its spectrum looks like, and why constant-amplitude forms resist noise better.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for sampling at fs ≥ 2fm, and Fourier series and spectra from Unit 1.

sections.h3: Pulse train, PAM and flat-top sampling

blocks.text: Take a periodic pulse train p(t) with period Ts = 1/fs, pulse width τ, and height A. The duty cycle is d = τ/Ts. The sampling rate must satisfy fs ≥ 2fm, as in Chapter 4.1; fm is the highest message frequency.

In pulse amplitude modulation (PAM), the height of each pulse follows the sample value: pulse k has height m(kT<sub>s</sub>). Natural PAM keeps the pulse shape and lets the top follow m(t). Flat-top PAM holds each sample constant for τ, so a sample-and-hold circuit can make it. The receiver recovers m(t) by low-pass filtering at f<sub>m</sub>.
P<sub>PAM</sub>(f) = (1/T<sub>s</sub>) Σ<sub>n</sub> M(f − n f<sub>s</sub>) · P(f)
blocks.where: P<sub>PAM</sub>(f) is the flat-top PAM spectrum; M(f) is the message spectrum; n is an integer; P(f) is the spectrum of one rectangular pulse: P(f) = A τ sinc(f τ), with sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx). For natural PAM the spectrum is Σ c<sub>n</sub> M(f − n f<sub>s</sub>) with c<sub>n</sub> = (τ/T<sub>s</sub>) sinc(n τ/T<sub>s</sub>), a weighted set of replicas, not M(f) multiplied by P(f).

blocks.text: The message spectrum repeats every fs, and the pulse shape acts as a low-pass filter. A flat-top pulse has nulls at f = 1/τ, 2/τ, … . This sinc attenuates high message frequencies; the loss is the aperture effect. An equalizer with a 1/sinc response can compensate. PAM is still an analog signal: it becomes digital only after quantization and coding, in Chapter 4.4.

PWM keeps the pulse height A fixed and varies the width. Pulse-duration modulation (PDM) is often the same thing; a few texts separate pulse-duration modulation (one edge fixed) from pulse-width modulation (both edges move). If the unmodulated width is τ<sub>0</sub>, then τ(t) = τ<sub>0</sub> + k<sub>w</sub> m(t), where k<sub>w</sub> is the width sensitivity in seconds per volt. The duty cycle d(t) = τ(t)/T<sub>s</sub> follows the message.

A comparator with a sawtooth reference at f<sub>s</sub> makes PWM. The comparator output is high while m(t) is above the sawtooth. A larger m(t) gives a wider high time. A low-pass filter averages the PWM wave and recovers m(t); the average is proportional to duty cycle.

Pulse-position modulation (PPM) keeps height and width fixed and slides the whole pulse earlier or later about its nominal slot by an amount proportional to m(t). Generate PPM from PWM by taking one edge per PWM period, usually the modulated trailing edge. A monostable, or a differentiator plus rectifier, turns that edge into one short pulse per PWM period. The pulse position then carries the sample.

PPM needs more bandwidth than PWM because narrow pulses have a wide sinc spectrum. PWM needs more bandwidth than PAM. Both PWM and PPM keep amplitude constant, so amplitude noise changes height less; timing jitter becomes the main error.
PAM, PWM and PPM differ in which pulse parameter carries the message.
PAM has the smallest bandwidth but is sensitive to amplitude noise. PWM and PPM trade bandwidth for noise immunity. PPM is the most bandwidth-hungry and needs good timing.
PAM also leads to multiplexing. Each pulse uses only τ of Ts, so samples from other signals can occupy the empty time. That is PAM-TDM, covered in Chapter 4.7.

figure.caption: The same message m(t) drives two paths: a sampler makes PAM, and a comparator with a sawtooth makes PWM; edge detection then converts PWM to PPM. Notice that only the pulse height changes in PAM, while the other two keep height fixed.

spec.title: From message to PAM, PWM, PPM
spec.aria: A common message drives a sampler to make PAM, and a comparator with a sawtooth to make PWM; an edge detector then turns PWM into PPM.

examples.question: A 1 kHz tone is sampled at 8 kHz. Each flat-top PAM pulse is 25 μs wide. Find the sampling interval, the duty cycle, and the first null of the pulse spectrum.
steps: Sampling interval: T<sub>s</sub> = 1/f<sub>s</sub> = 1/(8×10<sup>3</sup> Hz) = 125×10<sup>−6</sup> s = 125 μs.
Duty cycle: d = τ/T<sub>s</sub> = 25 μs / 125 μs = 0.20 = 20%.
First null: f<sub>null</sub> = 1/τ = 1/(25×10<sup>−6</sup> s) = 40×10<sup>3</sup> Hz = 40 kHz.
Check sampling: f<sub>s</sub> = 8 kHz > 2f<sub>m</sub> = 2 kHz, so no aliasing.
examples.answer: T<sub>s</sub> = 125 μs, duty cycle = 0.20 (20%), and the first null is at 40 kHz.
examples.check:
fs = 8000.0
tau = 25e-6
Ts = 1.0/fs
duty = tau/Ts
first_null_khz = (1.0/tau)/1000.0
print(Ts*1e6)
print(duty)
print(first_null_khz)

traps: PAM is not PCM. PAM is analog until quantization; PCM adds binary coding.
PPM shifts pulse position, not width; PWM changes width at constant height.
Duty cycle is τ/T<sub>s</sub>, not τ·T<sub>s</sub>, and it is dimensionless.
The first spectral null of a rectangular pulse is at 1/τ, not 1/(2τ).
Constant amplitude does not mean no noise; timing jitter and limited bandwidth still hurt PPM and PWM.

quiz.q: In PAM, which pulse parameter carries the message?
Why does flat-top PAM need an equalizer?
quiz.a: The rectangular hold gives a sinc spectrum with nulls at 1/τ, 2/τ, … . This sinc attenuates high message frequencies, the aperture effect, so an equalizer with a 1/sinc response restores them.

quiz.q: A 2 kHz tone is sampled at 10 kHz. Each rectangular pulse is 20 μs wide. Find T<sub>s</sub>, the duty cycle, and the first null.
Why are PWM and PPM more immune to amplitude noise than PAM?
quiz.a: PWM and PPM keep the pulse height constant. The receiver reads width or position, so amplitude noise changes only the height. PAM puts the message in the height, so the same noise adds directly to the recovered sample.

quiz.q: How is PPM generated from PWM?
quiz.a: Take one edge per PWM period, usually the modulated trailing edge. A monostable, or a differentiator plus rectifier, turns that edge into one short pulse per PWM period. The pulse position then carries the sample.

quiz.q: Order PAM, PWM and PPM by bandwidth, and explain the order.
quiz.a: PPM > PWM > PAM. Narrow PPM pulses need a wide sinc spectrum. PWM widths change slowly and need less. PAM pulses are the widest and need the least bandwidth.

quiz.q: A PAM wave has 10 μs pulses at f<sub>s</sub> = 20 kHz. Find the duty cycle.
When does PAM become a digital signal?
quiz.a: After quantization and binary coding, as in PCM; PAM itself is an analog pulse signal.

beyond: Not for the exam. PWM is everywhere in power electronics: class-D audio amplifiers, motor drives and LED dimming use it because the output stage is switched, not linear. PPM appears in optical and infrared links and in some ultra-wideband schemes. PAM4, a four-level PAM, carries two bits per symbol in high-speed serial links. Search next: class-D amplifier, PAM4 signalling, pulse position modulation optical.
